title: Services and Application Logic
learning_outcomes: Explain what services and application logic contributes to a PHP application.
Apply at least one of these concepts in a small example: service classes.
Check one edge case and explain how to diagnose unexpected behavior.

content.intro: Application architecture separates incoming requests, use-case rules, persistence, and external services. Patterns are useful when they clarify a dependency or invariant, not merely because they have a name. In this lesson, focus on service classes; then compare it with business operations. Use the example to predict a result before checking it, and record one case where the behavior may differ.
content.why_it_matters: You will use services and application logic when building readable, testable PHP programs. Its practical value is knowing which rule applies, what result to expect, and how to handle failure or unexpected input.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: Application architecture separates incoming requests, use-case rules, persistence, and external services. Patterns are useful when they clarify a dependency or invariant, not merely because they have a name. For services and application logic, begin with service classes. Also distinguish business operations; dependency boundaries; reusable application logic. Identify the input, the rule applied, and the observable output or side effect; then check the relevant official reference when a version or edge-case detail matters.

content_blocks.title: A small PHP example for Services and Application Logic
content_blocks.code:
<?php
final class Tax { public function amount(int $price): int { return intdiv($price, 10); } }
final class Checkout { public function __construct(private Tax $tax) {} public function total(int $price): int { return $price + $this->tax->amount($price); } }
echo (new Checkout(new Tax()))->total(100) . PHP_EOL;

content_blocks.title: Professional habit
content_blocks.text: Use the smallest representative example, make expected behavior explicit, and test normal plus boundary inputs.

content_blocks.title: Walk through one example
content_blocks.text: Read the example for services and application logic from top to bottom. Start by identifying service classes, write down the relevant variable values or control-flow choice, and predict the expected output before running it. Then change one input or condition, check a boundary case, and explain why the result changed.

hints: Start with the most direct listed subtopic and a single input.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying a pattern without understanding its inputs and output.
common_mistakes.why: Small environment or type differences can change behavior.
common_mistakes.fix: Trace one example by hand, name expected outputs, and consult version-matched official docs.

common_mistakes.problem: Ignoring empty, invalid, or boundary input.
common_mistakes.why: Real data rarely matches only the simplest example.
common_mistakes.fix: Add a deliberate edge-case check before relying on the result.

common_mistakes.problem: Making several changes at once while debugging.
common_mistakes.why: It becomes difficult to identify which change caused the behavior.
common_mistakes.fix: Reduce the issue to one small reproducible case, change one cause, and retest.
